Welcome to module four. So far in the course,
you've spent a lot of time evaluating what an agent says.

You've looked at responses, identified failures,
turned those failures into criteria,
and built evaluators that can apply those criteria to new examples.
But agents don't only produce responses.

They can retrieve information, make decisions, call tools,
and take actions that change something outside the conversation.

And once a task involves several of these steps,
a final response can look perfectly reasonable,
even when something went wrong along the way.

So let's go back to the shelter agent. Suppose a volunteer asks to go
on an outing with Pepper on Saturday afternoon.

The agent responds, "Great, you're booked with Pepper
for Saturday at 2 PM."
If you only evaluate that message, the interaction looks successful.

The response is clear, it confirms the dog, and it gives the right
time. But now open the trace and look at what the agent actually did.

It retrieved the volunteer's record, selected Pepper,
created the booking, and then sent the confirmation.

There's one problem: it never checked whether the volunteer was
eligible for the outing.

The booking may exist, the final message may even be
completely accurate,

but the agent skipped a step that the shelter requires before any
booking can be made.
That failure is almost impossible to see from the response alone.

You have to look at the work the agent did before it produced the
response. And a failure can start even earlier.

Imagine the agent receives a request from one volunteer,
but retrieves another volunteer's record by mistake.

From there, the rest of the run might actually look pretty good.
It checks the eligibility rules against the record it retrieved.

It selects a dog that is appropriate for that person.
It creates a valid booking.

Then it tells the user that the outing has been scheduled.
Each of those later steps can make sense on its own.
The problem is that they're all operating on the wrong volunteer.

So an error in one part of the workflow can propagate through
everything that follows
and still leave you with a polished final response.

This is why evaluating a task like this is different from
evaluating a single answer.
You need to look at the pieces of work that led to the answer.

For the shelter agent, that might mean checking the record it
retrieved, the eligibility decision it made, the action it took,
and finally, the response it gave the volunteer.
You don't necessarily need an evaluator for every internal step,

The question is which pieces of evidence can tell you whether the
requirements of the task were actually satisfied.

And looking at those pieces separately can also help you figure out
where a failure came from.

Go back to the case where the wrong volunteer record was retrieved.
Suppose the agent also makes a bad dog match.

If you only look at the final result, you know the match is wrong,
but you don't yet know why.

Maybe the matching logic itself is bad, or maybe it would have worked
if it had received the correct volunteer record.

One way to separate these possibilities is to evaluate that matching
decision again, using the correct record as the input.
If the agent now chooses an appropriate dog,

that gives you evidence that the matching logic can work and
that the earlier retrieval failure was driving the bad result.

If it still makes a bad match, then you've learned something else.
There may be a second problem in the reasoning itself.

So component-level evaluation helps you do more than say
that the overall task failed.

It helps you locate where the failure entered the process
and whether it spread into the steps that followed.

You'll use that idea throughout this module. As the tasks become more
complex, you'll look at different scopes of agent behavior.

Sometimes the important evidence is one action.
Sometimes it's the sequence of several actions.
Sometimes you need information from earlier turns in the conversation.

And sometimes the only way to know whether the task succeeded is to
check the state of the external system itself.

Northwind has the same challenge. The Northwind agent doesn't
just answer questions.

It can look up orders, retrieve customer information,
check product data, and issue refunds.
So imagine a customer asks for the status of an order.

Before you judge the final answer, there are already other questions
you might want to ask. Did the agent look up the right order?

Did it use the correct customer information?
If it took an action, was it actually the action the request required?
When an agent can choose among several possible actions,

you need to evaluate both what it decided to do and how it
carried that action out.
That's where we'll start in the next video.
